entry.evidence: We revisit his claims, replot his figures with recent data, simplify the use of his experimental tables

sequences.source_document: Vimal and Singh 2022, HESS 26, 445-467 (XML text and PDF)

steps.action: The authors take up Horton's 1917 claim that his physically based lake evaporation formula is an improvement over existing formulas.
steps.quote: Empirical Statement Based on Physical Law Agrees with Observed Facts and Is Held To Be an Improvement Over Existing Formulas

steps.action: They ask whether Horton's claim of an improved method holds today and why the method was overlooked or dismissed as empirical.
steps.quote: We revisit his claims, replot his figures with recent data, simplify the use of his experimental tables

steps.action: They merge existing bibliographies and run further searches to compile a list of 168 of Horton's works.
steps.quote: Combining these lists and conducting additional searches, the first author collated 168 works

steps.action: They review earlier treatments of Horton's equation (Chow 1964, Brutsaert 1982, McMahon et al. 2016, Singh and Xu 1997, Siomi and Yosida 1940) and judge them incomplete or incorrect.
steps.quote: in the few citations to them, the value and sophistication of the method was not recognized

steps.action: They trace Horton's theory sources (Dalton, Stevenson, Taylor and Shaw, Tate, Stefan, Risteen, Dolbear) through his citations and later papers.
steps.quote: A molecular kinetics view of evaporation is fundamental to Horton's approach

steps.action: They set out Horton's premise (kinetic theory; emission, removal and return of vapour) and his equations, in which a variable wind factor multiplies the water-surface vapour pressure (VVPD) in place of the VPD.
steps.quote: in Horton's equation for evaporation, the VPD term is replaced with a variable VPD term (VVPD)

steps.action: They extract Horton's 1927 and 1943b wind-factor and ground-wind tables with OCR software, convert them to parametric equations (2d-f, 3b-c), and use a bisection search to compute wind at other heights.
steps.quote: we converted them into the following equations for convenience

steps.action: Their first functional fits (R2 0.99) missed the high-velocity behaviour, so they adopted an improved two-parameter function found with outside help on Stack Overflow (R2 0.999).
steps.quote: However, the functions that provided this fit did not capture the high-velocity variations satisfactorily.

steps.action: Following Horton (1934), they factor the equation into a diffusion term and a vapour-removal term, so that barometric pressure acts on the diffusion term only (Eq. 8c).
steps.quote: By separating Eq. (8a) into its physically meaningful parts

steps.action: They take 30 min meteorological and evaporation data measured over and near a lake at Baker Creek, subarctic Canada (Spence and Hedstrom 2018), for 2009-2016.
steps.quote: We tested Horton's evaporation equation on Baker Creek in subarctic Canada, where 30 min meteorological data were available

steps.action: Following Singh and Xu (1997), they set five rival mass-transfer formulas against Horton's: Konstantinov, Dalton, Meyer, Rohwer, and the aerodynamic part of Penman.
steps.quote: following Singh and Xu (1997), we selected five other equations that resemble Horton's equation

steps.action: They calibrate all coefficients of all six formulas as free parameters over 1650 bootstrap samples (three record lengths, 50 resamples each, 11 timescales from 30 min to 2 months), recording mean and spread of R2 and percent bias.
steps.quote: We calibrated each of them by treating all the coefficients as free parameters

steps.action: They compare R2 and percent bias across methods and timescales (Table 1) and find Horton's formula the most accurate throughout.
steps.quote: Table 1 shows that Horton's method is substantially more accurate than the other methods

steps.action: Using relative performances reported by Tan et al. (2007), they place Horton's formula above radiation-, temperature- and combination-based model classes, with ANN models a possible exception.
steps.quote: as evidenced by relative performances reported in Tan et al. (2007)

steps.action: They replace observed vapour pressure with vapour pressure disaggregated from reanalysis-based data (MetSim/MTCLIM) and find that Horton's formula still outperforms the others, even against rivals given local measurements (Table 2).
steps.quote: Horton's method outperforms other methods, even when using the estimated input vapor pressure (Table 2)

steps.action: They compare the spread of the 17 calibrated parameters across bootstrap samples (Table 3) and find H = 1.71 with 1.3 % relative variability, the most stable of all.
steps.quote: parameter H has the most unchanging value (1.71) and the smallest (1.3 %) relative variability

steps.action: They compare the fitted H with Horton's and Dalton's value of 2 and with Schübler's (1831) wind-enhancement ratio of 1.7.
steps.quote: This value, interestingly, agrees very closely with Schübler's (1831) experimental observations

steps.action: They replot Horton's continental US longitude profiles of P, E and Q (from 112 pans) with Livneh et al. (2013) land-surface model output aggregated to 2 degree boxes, and find the curves remarkably similar.
steps.quote: Surprisingly, the curves for P , E , and Q are remarkably similar (see Fig. 2)

steps.action: They split the model data into three 30-year climate normals (1921-2010) to look for long-term change and find none, possibly because the dataset is detrended.
steps.quote: We further aggregated the data into three climate normals

steps.action: They attribute the substantial evaporation mismatch over the Great Lakes to auxiliaries (sunshine and cloud differences, masking of lake pixels in the model, lake-size effects) rather than to the method.
steps.quote: the land surface model results were masked out for the Great Lakes pixels

steps.action: They propose that the ratio E0/Ec and the near-constant H be named the Horton ratio and the Horton constant of lake evaporation.
steps.quote: These two points, we suggest, could be called the Horton ratio and the Horton constant for lake evaporation, respectively.

steps.action: They argue that Horton's equation can replace the rival formulas and the aerodynamic part of the Penman combination method, giving four reasons.
steps.quote: What we have shown here suggests that Horton's equation can indeed replace these other methods.

steps.action: They pose a new question: should the evaporation paradox be revisited using Horton's vapour-blanket and area-factor treatment of pans?
steps.quote: it seems that a revisit to explain the evaporation paradox is warranted

steps.action: They conclude that Horton's claim of a superior method still stands, and offer the parametric tables as a reference for wider use.
steps.quote: Horton's (1917a) claim of having developed a superior evaporation method (Eq. 1a–c) has as yet not been fully understood or proven wrong

Yes: lake evaporation is measured at Baker Creek (cited dataset)

tree.answer: Nature's repetitions stand in through bootstrap resamples and timescales at one site; no second lake
Survives a change of vapour-pressure input, record length and timescale; continental replot agrees except over the Great Lakes
Kept: Horton's formula fits best and H is nearly constant

end.claim: Horton's formula with the variable vapour pressure deficit outperforms five calibrated mass-transfer formulas at a subarctic lake across timescales, so his 1917 claim of a superior method stands.

decisive_move.sentence: The bootstrap comparison of the six calibrated formulas at Baker Creek (Table 1) is the only test on which the superiority claim rests; without it there is only historical exposition.

gates.evidence: Action: the aim of testing Horton's claim directed the choice of rivals and of an existing dataset (Baker Creek, Spence and Hedstrom 2018), but no data were acquired for the test (§4.1 ¶2). Claim: the calibrated rivals could have outfitted Horton's formula, and Rohwer's has more parameters (Table 3); the test is in-sample at one site (§4.1 ¶6). Registration: no hypothesis, metric or threshold is said to have been fixed before the data were seen, and the outlier criterion (10th percentile) is reported without a prior commitment (§4.3 ¶1).

imports.item: Molecular-kinetic picture of vapour emission, removal and return underlying Horton's formula
Clausius-Clapeyron relation for the saturation vapour pressure of the vapour blanket
Viscous sublayer analogy for the vapour blanket
Stefan's (1882) diffusion-evaporation derivation and its heat-conduction and electricity analogues
ExtractTable online scanning software to extract Horton's tables
Bisection search to invert the wind-height equation
Crowdsourced nonlinear two-parameter function fit (Vimal and Mikuszeit 2021)
Bootstrap resampling with replacement to obtain means and spreads of R2, bias and parameters

novelty_claims.quote: the first author collated 168 works, which is the most comprehensive list of Horton's works available to [...]
They have not been collectively examined in any previous work to [...]
To our knowledge, wind's role on vapor removal as an exhaustion process has not been studied by other investigators.
To our knowledge, there is no other evaporation formulation that captures the role of H
It appears that Horton provided the first quantitative treatment highlighting the importance of these two values for lakes.

limits: Headline claim at best_explanation: the test uses one lake (Baker Creek) with mostly summer coverage. All six formulas are calibrated in-sample on bootstrap resamples of the same record, with no held-out period or second site. The authors themselves say they 'do not draw bald conclusions' before testing at multiple lakes (§4.1 ¶6), yet the abstract and conclusions state superiority broadly. The rivals' wind inputs were back-calculated with the authors' own Eq. 3b; they name this as a possible reason for the rivals' poorer performance (§4.1 ¶6), so the comparison may be biased in Horton's favour (inference). The continental check (Figure 2) compares Horton's 1943 pan-based profiles with Livneh model output. The text does not show that Horton's formula, as parametrized here, produced those profiles, so the claim that it 'generalize[s] over continental scales' (§4.5 ¶2) is weakly supported (inference); the Great Lakes mismatch is explained by auxiliaries rather than tested. Sub-claims: H = 1.71 with 1.3 % relative variability is estimate_with_resolution, conditional on one site and on outlier removal at the 10th percentile; the parametric versions of Horton's tables (R2 0.999) are capability_characterized; the Horton constant and Horton ratio, Penman replacement and evaporation-paradox claims are proposals without a test (status none). The abstract's '3 %-15 % of R2' and 'order of magnitude' figures are read off Tables 1-2, which exist only as images; the coder relied on the PDF rendering. No peer-review file, discussion or earlier version was supplied, so no review sequence is coded, although the acknowledgements say the editor (Beven) commented extensively. Code is available on request only. Much of the paper (§1-§3, §7) is historical exposition, coded as synthesis steps.

disagreements.support: They argue the wind factor must multiply the water-surface vapour pressure, not the whole deficit, so the earlier evaluation of Horton's equation was invalid.
disagreements.quote: Singh and Xu (1997) evaluated Horton's evaporation equation in comparison with 12 other (mostly) empirical equations that resemble it, [...]

disagreements.target: Rohwer (1931) and investigators who dubbed Horton's formula empirical or of small practical value
disagreements.support: They reconstruct the formula's derivation from physical premises and show its constant H is the most stable parameter across bootstrap samples, with the best fit at Baker Creek.
disagreements.quote: several investigators may have dubbed it as simply empirical (see Rohwer, 1931)

disagreements.target: Brutsaert (1982) treatise and the mainstream evaporation literature that omitted Horton
disagreements.support: They document the omission and argue, from the comparative test, that the method deserved inclusion.
disagreements.quote: Horton's formula is surprisingly not included in Brutsaert's (1982) treatise

disagreements.target: Dalton-type formulas with a linear wind factor (f(u) = 1 + Kw)
disagreements.support: They restate Horton's argument that wind cannot remove vapour faster than it is emitted, and show the bounded-wind-factor formula fits better than calibrated linear-wind formulas.
disagreements.quote: Most existing evaporation formulas are in error in that they involve a linear factor for wind correction

disagreements.target: Horton's and Dalton's value H = 2 and Horton's wind coefficient k = 0.2-0.3
disagreements.support: Bootstrap calibration gives H = 1.71 and k = 0.13 (Table 3), close to Schübler's ratio of 1.7.
disagreements.quote: Horton assigned it a constant value of 2, but it could be a little lower (discussed in Sect. 4)

disagreements.support: Converting both tables shows the 1943b values differ slightly from those of 1927.
disagreements.quote: The table values for Ψ might possibly be an error in Horton (1943b)

disagreements.support: No long-term change appears across three climate normals; they suspect the dataset is detrended.
disagreements.quote: This could possibly be an inherent issue with the Livneh et al. (2013) dataset, which possibly is detrended.

disagreements.target: Penman combination method and VPD-based aerodynamic terms in land-surface modelling
disagreements.support: They argue from the Baker Creek results, the separability of pressure effects, and errors in energy-balance inputs (albedo, radiation), but run no direct test against the full combination method.
disagreements.quote: These arguments make a strong case for favoring Horton's equation over the combination method for both large and small lakes.

disagreements.target: Pan-based studies of the evaporation paradox using static pan coefficients (Bouchet complementarity line; Doorenbos and Pruitt 1977)
disagreements.support: They argue that Horton's vapour-blanket and area-factor treatment shows static pan corrections are inadequate; the argument is conceptual and untested here.
disagreements.quote: it would be quite wrong to use a simple, static pan correction parameter (Horton, 1917a)
